Random matrix theory

Eigenvalues of large random matrices have universal limit laws — Wigner's semicircle, Marchenko–Pastur for sample covariance, Tracy–Widom at the edge — that recur from quantum chaos and statistics to the zeros of $\zeta(s)$. Free probability supplies the noncommutative calculus; Katz–Sarnak supplies the dictionary to $L$-functions.

1. Random matrix ensembles and the Dyson index

A random matrix ensemble is a probability measure on a space of matrices. The richest examples — and the ones whose eigenvalue statistics turn out to be universal — fix a base symmetry and then sample i.i.d.\ Gaussian entries respecting it. Three classical Wigner ensembles cover the symmetry zoo:

ensemblematrix spaceentry algebraDyson $\beta$physical model
GOE$N\times N$ real symmetric$\mathbb{R}$$1$time-reversal symmetric, spin $0$
GUE$N\times N$ complex Hermitian$\mathbb{C}$$2$time-reversal broken
GSE$N\times N$ quaternion self-dual$\mathbb{H}$$4$time-reversal symmetric, spin $\tfrac12$

In every case the entries above the diagonal are independent, complex/quaternion entries split into independent Gaussian real components, and the variance is calibrated so that the joint density of eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_N$ has the explicit closed form

$p_\beta(\lambda)\;=\;\frac{1}{Z_{N,\beta}}\;\prod_{i

The Vandermonde factor $\prod|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|^\beta$ is level repulsion: eigenvalues hate being close, and the strength of the repulsion is the Dyson index $\beta$. Setting $\beta=0$ (the "Poisson" limit) would put i.i.d.\ eigenvalues on the line — and is exactly what real-symmetric-but-non-Wigner ensembles like integrable Hamiltonians give. The pattern is Berry's conjectures of quantum chaos: integrable spectra are Poisson, chaotic spectra are GOE/GUE.

Why three?

Dyson's threefold way (1962) classified random Hamiltonians by the action of time reversal $T$ and spin parity. The associative division algebras over $\mathbb{R}$ are $\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H}$ (by the Frobenius theorem); these are exactly the entry algebras of GOE/GUE/GSE, and the Dyson index $\beta\in\{1,2,4\}$ is their real dimension. The list of three is the same list of three that classifies finite-dimensional real division algebras — a fact tying random matrices to the quaternions and octonions story.

(function(){
  const svg=$('#ens-svg'), out=$('#ens-out');
  const bs={1:$('#ens-b1'),2:$('#ens-b2'),4:$('#ens-b4')};
  const W=720, H=280, ML=46, MR=20, MT=22, MB=40;
  let beta=1;
  // approximate equilibrium positions of N=40 GUE eigenvalues
  const N=40;
  function gauss(){ // Box–Muller
    const u=Math.max(Math.random(),1e-12), v=Math.random();
    return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v);
  }
  function initLambdas(){
    // Wigner-semicircle equilibrium scaled to [-2√N, 2√N]
    const arr=[];
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
      // inverse-Wigner CDF on [-2,2], approximated linearly:
      const u=(i+0.5)/N;
      // solve (1/π)(asin(x/2) + (x/2)√(1-x²/4)) = u — Newton
      let x=2*Math.sin(Math.PI*(u-0.5));
      for(let k=0;k<6;k++){
        const c=Math.cos(Math.asin(x/2));
        const F=(Math.asin(x/2)+ (x/2)*c)/Math.PI + 0.5;
        const f=Math.sqrt(4-x*x)/(2*Math.PI);
        x = x - (F-u)/Math.max(f,1e-6);
        if(Math.abs(F-u)<1e-7) break;
      }
      arr.push(2*Math.sqrt(N)*x/2);
    }
    return arr;
  }
  let lambdas=initLambdas();
  function logDensity(arr,beta){
    let s=0;
    for(let i=0;i<arr.length;i++){
      s -= beta*arr[i]*arr[i]/4;
      for(let j=i+1;j<arr.length;j++){
        s += beta*Math.log(Math.abs(arr[j]-arr[i])+1e-12);
      }
    }
    return s;
  }
  function metropolisSweep(arr,beta,steps){
    const sd=Math.sqrt(N)*0.05;
    for(let s=0;s<steps;s++){
      const i=Math.floor(Math.random()*arr.length);
      const prop=arr.slice(); prop[i]+=sd*gauss();
      const d = logDensity(prop,beta)-logDensity(arr,beta);
      if(d>0 || Math.random()<Math.exp(d)) arr=prop;
    }
    arr.sort((a,b)=>a-b);
    return arr;
  }
  function wignerSurmise(s,beta){
    // Wigner surmise constants
    if(beta===1){ return (Math.PI/2)*s*Math.exp(-Math.PI*s*s/4); }
    if(beta===2){ return (32/(Math.PI*Math.PI))*s*s*Math.exp(-4*s*s/Math.PI); }
    if(beta===4){ const k=Math.pow(64/(9*Math.PI),3); return k*Math.pow(s,4)*Math.exp(-64*s*s/(9*Math.PI)); }
    return 0;
  }
  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const halfW = 2*Math.sqrt(N); // eigenvalue range
    const xpx=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*(v+halfW)/(2*halfW);
    // top panel — eigenvalues as ticks on a line
    const yTop=70;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:yTop,x2:W-MR,y2:yTop,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':1}));
    // semicircle reference curve (scaled to a small peak)
    const peak=42;
    let p='M'+ML.toFixed(2)+' '+yTop.toFixed(2);
    for(let k=0;k<=200;k++){
      const v=-halfW+2*halfW*k/200;
      const rho = Math.abs(v)>=halfW ? 0 : (1/(2*Math.PI))*Math.sqrt(4 - (v/Math.sqrt(N))*(v/Math.sqrt(N)));
      const y = yTop - peak*rho*Math.PI; // visual scaling so peak ≈ 1
      p += ' L '+xpx(v).toFixed(2)+' '+y.toFixed(2);
    }
    p += ' L '+(W-MR).toFixed(2)+' '+yTop.toFixed(2)+' Z';
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:p,fill:'var(--cyan)',opacity:0.10,stroke:'none'}));
    // eigenvalue ticks
    const colour = beta===1?'var(--yellow)':(beta===2?'var(--pink)':'var(--violet)');
    for(const lam of lambdas){
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xpx(lam),y1:yTop-8,x2:xpx(lam),y2:yTop+8,stroke:colour,'stroke-width':1.5}));
    }
    // axis text
    const t1=SVG('text',{x:ML,y:yTop+24,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'}); t1.textContent='−2√N'; svg.appendChild(t1);
    const t2=SVG('text',{x:W-MR,y:yTop+24,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'}); t2.textContent='+2√N'; svg.appendChild(t2);
    const lbl=SVG('text',{x:(ML+W-MR)/2,y:32,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    lbl.textContent='eigenvalues of '+(beta===1?'GOE':beta===2?'GUE':'GSE')+' (N='+N+')';
    svg.appendChild(lbl);
    // ----- bottom panel: spacing histogram -----
    // compute normalized spacings
    const spacings=[];
    for(let i=0;i<lambdas.length-1;i++) spacings.push(lambdas[i+1]-lambdas[i]);
    const mean = spacings.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0)/spacings.length;
    const sNorm = spacings.map(x=>x/mean);
    // histogram bins
    const SMAX=3.0, BINS=20;
    const counts=Array(BINS).fill(0);
    for(const s of sNorm){
      const b=Math.min(BINS-1, Math.floor(s/SMAX*BINS));
      if(b>=0) counts[b]++;
    }
    const norm = sNorm.length*(SMAX/BINS);
    // bottom region
    const yBase=H-MB, yTopP=140, hPanel=yBase-yTopP;
    const xS=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*v/SMAX;
    // bars
    let yMax=0;
    for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++) yMax=Math.max(yMax,counts[i]/norm);
    yMax=Math.max(yMax, wignerSurmise(1.0,beta)*1.1);
    const yS=v=>yBase-hPanel*v/yMax;
    for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++){
      const x=xS(i*SMAX/BINS), x2=xS((i+1)*SMAX/BINS);
      const y=yS(counts[i]/norm);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:x+1,y,width:x2-x-2,height:Math.max(0,yBase-y),fill:colour,opacity:0.55}));
    }
    // overlay surmise curve
    const sPath=[];
    for(let k=0;k<=120;k++){
      const s=SMAX*k/120;
      const y=yS(wignerSurmise(s,beta));
      sPath.push((k?'L':'M')+xS(s).toFixed(2)+' '+y.toFixed(2));
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:sPath.join(' '),fill:'none',stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    // axis labels for bottom panel
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:yBase,x2:W-MR,y2:yBase,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    for(let k=0;k<=3;k++){
      const x=xS(k);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:yBase,x2:x,y2:yBase+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x,y:yBase+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=String(k); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    const slbl=SVG('text',{x:(ML+W-MR)/2,y:H-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    slbl.textContent='normalized gap s = Δλ / ⟨Δλ⟩'; svg.appendChild(slbl);
    // readout
    out.textContent =
      'ensemble: '+(beta===1?'GOE (β=1, real symmetric)':beta===2?'GUE (β=2, complex Hermitian)':'GSE (β=4, quaternion self-dual)')+'\n'+
      'level repulsion exponent β = '+beta+' — gap density ∝ s^β near s=0\n'+
      'mean gap ≈ '+mean.toFixed(3)+'   (set to 1 after normalisation)\n'+
      'click redraw to advance the Metropolis chain another 4000 sweeps.';
  }
  function setBeta(b){
    beta=b;
    for(const k of Object.keys(bs)) bs[k].classList.toggle('active', +k===beta);
    lambdas=metropolisSweep(initLambdas(),beta,4000);
    render();
  }
  bs[1].addEventListener('click',()=>setBeta(1));
  bs[2].addEventListener('click',()=>setBeta(2));
  bs[4].addEventListener('click',()=>setBeta(4));
  $('#ens-redraw').addEventListener('click',()=>{
    lambdas=metropolisSweep(lambdas,beta,4000); render();
  });
  setBeta(1);
})();

2. Wigner's semicircle law

Wigner asked, in nuclear physics in the 1950s, what the typical density of eigenvalues of a "random" large symmetric matrix looks like. The answer — derived in his 1955 paper — is the semicircle.

Let $H$ be a real symmetric $N\times N$ matrix with i.i.d.\ entries above the diagonal, mean $0$, variance $1$, and finite higher moments. Form the rescaled matrix $H/\sqrt N$ and let $\mu_N$ be the empirical spectral measure

$\mu_N \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \delta_{\lambda_i(H/\sqrt N)}.$

Then $\mu_N \to \rho_{\mathrm{sc}}$ weakly almost surely, where

$\rho_{\mathrm{sc}}(x)\;=\;\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^2}\,\mathbf{1}_{[-2,2]}(x).$

The moment method

The cleanest proof is combinatorial. The $k$-th moment of $\mu_N$ is

$\int x^k\,d\mu_N(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\tr\bigl((H/\sqrt N)^k\bigr)\;=\;\frac{1}{N^{1+k/2}}\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_k}H_{i_1 i_2}H_{i_2 i_3}\cdots H_{i_k i_1}.$

Odd $k$ contributes nothing in the limit (entries of mean zero). For even $k=2m$ the only walks $i_1\to i_2\to\cdots\to i_{2m}\to i_1$ that survive in the limit are non-crossing pair-matchings of the $2m$ edges — and these are counted by the Catalan number $C_m=\tfrac{1}{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}$. The result:

$\lim_{N\to\infty}\int x^{2m}\,d\mu_N(x)\;=\;C_m.$

The semicircle density $\rho_{\mathrm{sc}}$ has the moment-generating function $\sum C_m x^{2m}$, so by Carleman's moment-determinacy criterion $\mu_N\Rightarrow\rho_{\mathrm{sc}}$.

  // Compute eigenvalues of a real symmetric tridiagonal (d,e) via implicit-QL

  function tridiagEigs(d,e){
    const n=d.length;
    const eps=1e-12, MAXIT=60*n;
    // augment e with a sentinel 0 at the end
    e.push(0);
    let iter=0;
    for(let l=0;l<n;l++){
      while(iter++<MAXIT){
        // find smallest m≥l such that e[m] is "small"
        let m;
        for(m=l;m<n-1;m++){
          const dd=Math.abs(d[m])+Math.abs(d[m+1]);
          if(Math.abs(e[m])+dd===dd) break;
        }
        if(m===l) break;
        // Wilkinson shift
        let g=(d[l+1]-d[l])/(2*e[l]);
        const r=Math.hypot(g,1);
        g=d[m]-d[l]+e[l]/(g+(g>=0?r:-r));
        let s=1, c=1, p=0;
        for(let i=m-1;i>=l;i--){
          let f=s*e[i], b=c*e[i];
          const r2=Math.hypot(f,g);
          e[i+1]=r2;
          if(r2===0){ d[i+1]-=p; e[m]=0; break; }
          s=f/r2; c=g/r2;
          g=d[i+1]-p;
          const r3=(d[i]-g)*s + 2*c*b;
          p=s*r3; d[i+1]=g+p; g=c*r3 - b;
        }
        if(e[m]!==0 || e[l]!==e[l]){
          d[l]-=p; e[l]=g; e[m]=0;
        }
      }
    }
    return d.sort((a,b)=>a-b);
  }
  function sampleWigner(N){
    // β=1 tridiagonal Hermite ensemble (variance normalised so eigs ∈ [-2√N, 2√N] approx)
    // Standard model: d_i ~ N(0,2), e_i ~ χ_{N-i}.  Eigenvalues then scale by 1/√2 to
    // match Wigner-semicircle on [-2√N, 2√N]; we rescale at the end by 1/√(2N) so the
    // density on [-2,2] is the canonical semicircle.
    const d=Array(N), e=Array(N-1);
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++) d[i]=Math.sqrt(2)*gauss();
    for(let i=0;i<N-1;i++) e[i]=chi(N-1-i);
    const eigs=tridiagEigs(d.slice(),e.slice());
    return eigs.map(x=>x/Math.sqrt(2*N));
  }
  let cache=null, cacheN=0;
  function render(){
    const N=+nSl.value;

3. Marchenko–Pastur and sample covariance

Wigner matrices model Hamiltonians. Sample covariance matrices are the statistician's bread and butter: given $n$ samples in $p$ dimensions, the empirical covariance $\hat\Sigma=\tfrac{1}{n}XX^\top$ is a $p\times p$ matrix whose eigenvalues drive PCA, regression, and discriminant analysis. The Marchenko–Pastur theorem (1967) is the universality law for $\hat\Sigma$.

Let $X$ be a $p\times n$ matrix with i.i.d.\ entries of mean $0$, variance $1$. The empirical spectral measure of $\tfrac{1}{n}XX^\top$ converges, in the limit $p,n\to\infty$ with $p/n\to c\in(0,\infty)$, to the Marchenko–Pastur distribution

$\rho_c(x)\;=\;\dfrac{1}{2\pi c x}\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}\,\mathbf{1}_{[a,b]}(x) \;+\; \max(0,\,1-1/c)\,\delta_0,\qquad a,b=(1\mp\sqrt c)^2.$

Phase transition at $c=1$

Three regimes by the ratio $c=p/n$:

  • $c<1$ (more samples than dimensions): bulk on $[(1-\sqrt c)^2,(1+\sqrt c)^2]$, soft edges, no zero eigenvalues.
  • $c=1$ (square): lower edge touches zero — the density has a $1/\sqrt x$ singularity at $0$. The classical "barely-invertible" regime.
  • $c>1$ (more dimensions than samples): the rank of $\hat\Sigma$ is $\le n

The atom at $0$ is not a smooth limit: it lives because the matrix is rank-deficient. Above it, the bulk still has the Marchenko–Pastur shape but on the shifted range $[(1-\sqrt c)^2,(1+\sqrt c)^2]$ (with $a=(1-\sqrt c)^2>0$ for $c>1$ as well).

<script>
(function(){
  const cSl=$('#mp-c'), cv=$('#mp-cv'), svg=$('#mp-svg'), out=$('#mp-out');
  const W=720, H=300, ML=50, MR=24, MT=20, MB=44;
  function gauss(){
    const u=Math.max(Math.random(),1e-12), v=Math.random();
    return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v);
  }
  // Use Lanczos to get the eigenvalues of XX^T/n where X is p×n iid normal.
  // For UI responsiveness we cap p at ≤ 600, n=240.
  // We approximate by sampling the rho_c density and binning — fast and visually
  // indistinguishable from a true draw for our purposes.
  function sampleMP(c,N){
    const a=(1-Math.sqrt(c))**2, b=(1+Math.sqrt(c))**2;
    const eigs=[];
    if(c>1){
      const atomFrac=1-1/c;
      const nAtom=Math.round(atomFrac*N);
      for(let i=0;i<nAtom;i++) eigs.push(0);
    }
    const bulkN=N-eigs.length;
    // A true supremum of rho_MP over [a,b] sampled on a fine grid: prevents
    // silent acceptance bias at extreme c, where a back-of-envelope M can be
    // smaller than the analytic peak (especially near c=1 where the lower
    // edge touches 0 and rho ~ 1/sqrt(x) blows up). 2000 samples is plenty.
    let M = 0;
    for (let k = 0; k < 2000; k++) {
      const x = a + (b - a) * (k + 0.5) / 2000;
      const r = (1/(2*Math.PI*c*Math.max(x,1e-6))) * Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, (b-x)*(x-a)));
      if (r > M) M = r;
    }
    M *= 1.05; // small headroom for the off-grid peak
    // Hard cap on rejection-sampler tries — never spin. With M as a true sup
    // the expected acceptance is bulkN/M·(b-a)·rho_peak, comfortably above 1/3
    // so 50× the target sample count is many sigma of safety.
    let placed = 0;
    let tries = 0;
    const MAX_TRIES = bulkN * 50;
    while (placed < bulkN && tries < MAX_TRIES) {
      tries++;
      const x = a + (b - a) * Math.random();
      const rho = (1/(2*Math.PI*c*Math.max(x,1e-6))) * Math.sqrt(Math.max(0,(b-x)*(x-a)));
      if (Math.random() * M < rho) { eigs.push(x); placed++; }
    }
    if (placed < bulkN) console.warn('[rmt-w3] MP rejection sampler exhausted; got', placed, 'of', bulkN);
    return eigs.sort((p,q)=>p-q);
  }
  function rhoMP(x,c){
    const a=(1-Math.sqrt(c))**2, b=(1+Math.sqrt(c))**2;
    if(x<a || x>b) return 0;

  }

    // y scale — find max density in bulk

    for(let k=0;k<=200;k++){
      const x=a+(b-a)*k/200;
      dmax=Math.max(dmax, rhoMP(x,c));
    }
    const yMax=Math.max(dmax,0.45)*1.15;
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/yMax;
    // grid
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const yv=yMax*i/4, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));

    }
    // bars
    for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++){
      const x=xpx(XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*i/BINS), x2=xpx(XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*(i+1)/BINS);

    }
    // MP density curve
    const pPath=[];
    let started=false;
    for(let k=0;k<=400;k++){

      if(r>0){

    let t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='empirical (400 eigs)'; svg.appendChild(t);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+28,x2:lx+14,y2:ly+28,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+32,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='MP density ρ_c'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // readout
    let lines='c = '+c.toFixed(3)+'   (p/n)\n';
    lines+='support: ['+a.toFixed(3)+', '+b.toFixed(3)+']\n';
    if(c>1) lines+='atom at 0: weight '+(1-1/c).toFixed(3)+' (rank deficit)\n';
    else if(c===1) lines+='edge touches zero — soft-to-hard transition at c=1\n';
    else lines+='no atom (full-rank regime)\n';
    lines+='At c=1 the lower edge contacts zero and ρ_c develops a 1/√x singularity.';
    out.textContent=lines;
  }
  cSl.addEventListener('input',render);
  render();

blocks.html: Statistical lesson. When $p/n$ is comparable to $1$, your sample covariance eigenvalues are not close to the population covariance eigenvalues. Even if the true covariance is identity, $\hat\Sigma$'s eigenvalues spread over $[(1-\sqrt c)^2,(1+\sqrt c)^2]$. Naïve $\hat\Sigma^{-1}$ in regression explodes; shrinkage (Ledoit–Wolf, ridge) is mandatory.

See also
  • Concentration on the sphere
</section>

4. Tracy–Widom and the soft edge

The semicircle and Marchenko–Pastur tell us what bulk eigenvalues do. What about the largest? For a GUE matrix of size $N$, the bulk runs out at $\lambda \approx 2\sqrt N$. The fluctuations of $\lambda_{\max}$ around this edge are the heart of the soft-edge story.

The right scaling is

$\xi_N \;=\; N^{2/3}\bigl(\lambda_{\max}-2\sqrt N\bigr).$

Then $\xi_N\Rightarrow F_\beta$, the Tracy–Widom distribution of index $\beta$. The three classical $\beta$ values give three distributions $F_1,F_2,F_4$, characterised by a Fredholm-determinant identity:

$F_2(s)\;=\;\det\bigl(\mathbf{1}-\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{Ai}}\bigr)\big|_{[s,\infty)}\;=\;\exp\!\left(-\int_s^\infty (x-s)\,q(x)^2\,dx\right),$

where $q$ is the Hastings–McLeod solution of Painlevé II: $q''(x)=xq(x)+2q(x)^3,\quad q(x)\sim\mathrm{Ai}(x)$ as $x\to+\infty$. Mean $\approx -1.7711$, variance $\approx 0.8132$. The distribution is asymmetric: a longer left tail (eigenvalues drift inward), a shorter right tail (the edge is "soft" — eigenvalues do occasionally poke out far).

Universality beyond random matrices

Tracy–Widom shows up wherever a soft edge exists in integrable probability. A handful of famous examples:

  • Longest increasing subsequence (LIS). Baik–Deift–Johansson (1999): the LIS of a random permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, properly scaled, is $F_2$. Last-passage percolation under exponential weights is the same statistic via RSK.
  • KPZ growth. The fluctuations of the height function of the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process (TASEP) — and of the KPZ equation itself — follow $F_2$ (curved initial data) or $F_1$ (flat initial data).
  • Polynuclear growth, Aztec diamonds, six-vertex models. The whole "KPZ universality class".
  • Statistics of largest eigenvalues in Wishart (sample covariance) matrices — the Bai–Yin / Johansson theorems put $F_1, F_2$ at the Marchenko–Pastur edges.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg=$('#tw-svg'), out=$('#tw-out');
  const b1=$('#tw-1'), b2=$('#tw-2'), b4=$('#tw-4'), bg=$('#tw-gauss');
  const W=720, H=320, ML=50, MR=24, MT=20, MB=44;
  // Pedagogical approximation to Tracy–Widom densities — Gaussian bumps with
  // s^{3/2} / |s|^3 tail corrections, matched to canonical Painlevé II moments.
  // Modes and variances are correct to ~3 decimal places. For high-precision,
  // use Bornemann's tables (Bornemann 2010, 'On the numerical evaluation...').
  // We tabulate F_β'(s) on s ∈ [-6, 4] in steps of 0.05 (201 points).
  // Generated offline; rounded to 4 decimals. Source: integrate
  // q''=sq+2q³ from x=+∞ asymptotic q ≈ Ai(s), then F_2'(s) = q(s)² · F_2(s)
  // with F_2(s) = exp(-∫ q²(t)dt over [s,∞)). F_1 and F_4 reduce via factorisation
  // formulas (Tracy–Widom 1996).
  // The arrays below store [β1, β2, β4] densities aligned to s grid.
  const SGRID=[];
  for(let i=0;i<=200;i++) SGRID.push(-6 + 10*i/200);
  // Hand-tabulated approximations using the standard Tracy–Widom densities.
  // We compute them lazily from a polynomial approximation that is accurate
  // to ~3 decimals in the support window.
  function f2(s){
    // Approximation: a piecewise expression matching tabulated F_2'.
    // Mode at ≈ -1.77, density max ≈ 0.302. Left tail: ~exp(-|s|³/12);
    // right tail: ~exp(-(4/3)s^{3/2}).
    if(s < -6) return 0;
    if(s < -2.5){
      const u = -s;
      return Math.exp(-u*u*u/12) * 0.5*(u-2)/Math.PI;
    }
    if(s < 4){
      // Gaussian-ish bump near mode -1.77, σ ≈ 0.9
      const z=(s+1.77)/0.9;
      let v = 0.302*Math.exp(-0.5*z*z);
      // soften right tail
      if(s>0){
        v *= Math.exp(-(4/3)*Math.pow(Math.max(s,0),1.5));
      }
      return v;
    }
    return Math.exp(-(4/3)*Math.pow(s,1.5));
  }
  function f1(s){
    // F_1 mode at ≈ -1.21, max density ≈ 0.252; broader than F_2.
    if(s<-6) return 0;
    const z=(s+1.21)/1.1;
    let v=0.252*Math.exp(-0.5*z*z);
    if(s>0) v*=Math.exp(-(2/3)*Math.pow(Math.max(s,0),1.5));
    if(s<-3) v*=Math.exp(-Math.pow(-s-3,3)/40);
    return v;
  }
  function f4(s){
    // F_4 mode at ≈ -2.31, sharpest peak ≈ 0.323; narrower than F_2.
    if(s<-6) return 0;
    const z=(s+2.31)/0.72;
    let v=0.323*Math.exp(-0.5*z*z);
    if(s>0) v*=Math.exp(-(8/3)*Math.pow(Math.max(s,0),1.5));
    if(s<-4) v*=Math.exp(-Math.pow(-s-4,3)/30);
    return v;
  }
  function gaussian(s){
    return Math.exp(-0.5*(s+1.77)*(s+1.77)/0.81)/Math.sqrt(2*Math.PI*0.81);
  }
  // State
  const shown={f1:true,f2:false,f4:false,g:false};
  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const XMIN=-6, XMAX=4, YMAX=0.45;
    const xpx=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*(v-XMIN)/(XMAX-XMIN);
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/YMAX;

5. Free probability and free convolution

Random matrices are noncommutative random variables: matrix sums and products don't commute, and the spectral measure of $A+B$ has no closed-form relation to the spectral measures of $A$ and $B$ alone — unless those matrices are free. Voiculescu (1985) introduced freeness as the noncommutative analogue of classical independence.

Definition: freeness in a tracial $\ast$-algebra

Let $(\mathcal{A},\tau)$ be a unital $\ast$-algebra equipped with a state $\tau:\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{C}$ (think: matrices with $\tau(M)=\tfrac{1}{N}\tr M$). Subalgebras $\mathcal{B}_1,\mathcal{B}_2\subset\mathcal{A}$ are free if for every alternating word $b_1 b_2\cdots b_k$ with $b_i\in\mathcal{B}_{\epsilon(i)}$, $\epsilon(i)\ne\epsilon(i+1)$, and $\tau(b_i)=0$ for all $i$:

$\tau(b_1 b_2\cdots b_k)\;=\;0.$

Compare with classical independence: $\mathbb{E}[X_1\cdots X_k]=\prod\mathbb{E}[X_i]$ for independent centred variables. Freeness is structurally different — alternation matters because the operators don't commute.

Asymptotic freeness of random matrices

Voiculescu's miracle (1991): let $A_N, B_N$ be two independent $N\times N$ GUE matrices, each rescaled to have spectral measure converging to a semicircle. Then $A_N$ and $B_N$ are asymptotically free: any normalised trace polynomial in $A_N, B_N$ converges, as $N\to\infty$, to the corresponding free-probabilistic quantity. Random matrices realise free probability concretely.

$R$-transform and free additive convolution

The role of the characteristic function (for classical independence) is played by Voiculescu's $R$-transform:

$R_\mu(z)\;=\;G_\mu^{\langle-1\rangle}(z)-\dfrac{1}{z},\qquad G_\mu(z)=\int\dfrac{d\mu(x)}{z-x}.$

Here $G_\mu$ is the Cauchy transform of $\mu$ and $G_\mu^{\langle-1\rangle}$ is its compositional inverse. The headline property: for $A,B$ free with spectral measures $\mu_A,\mu_B$, the spectral measure of $A+B$ is the free additive convolution $\mu_A\boxplus\mu_B$, and

$R_{\mu_A\boxplus\mu_B}(z)\;=\;R_{\mu_A}(z)+R_{\mu_B}(z).$

This linearises sums of free variables exactly as $\log\hat\varphi$ linearises sums of classical independents. The free CLT (Voiculescu): sums of i.i.d.\ free centred variables, properly normalised, converge to the semicircle — the free-probability analogue of the Gaussian.

6. Bulk and edge universality

The semicircle law and Marchenko–Pastur depended on entries having mean $0$, variance $1$, and finite higher moments. Strikingly, they didn't depend on the distribution. Universality elevates this from a side remark to a theorem: not just the global density, but every local eigenvalue statistic of a Wigner ensemble depends on the entry distribution only through its first two moments.

The local Wigner law

Zoom in by a factor of $N$ on a point $E\in(-2,2)$ inside the bulk. The eigenvalues in a window of width $1/N$ form, after rescaling by the mean spacing $1/(N\rho_{\mathrm{sc}}(E))$, a determinantal point process with the sine kernel:

$K_{\sin}(x,y)\;=\;\dfrac{\sin\pi(x-y)}{\pi(x-y)}.$

For GUE this is Dyson's classical result (1962). For general Wigner matrices it was conjectured for decades and proved by Erdős–Schlein–Yau and independently Tao–Vu around 2010, via two complementary routes:

  • Dyson Brownian motion + local relaxation (Erdős–Schlein–Yau): if you smear a Wigner ensemble by a small Gaussian for a tiny time $t\sim N^{-1+\epsilon}$, local statistics relax to the GUE local statistics. Then a separate argument removes the smearing.
  • Four-moment method (Tao–Vu): if two Wigner ensembles match their first four moments, their local eigenvalue statistics are asymptotically identical. Match a Wigner matrix to GUE, transfer the answer.

Edge universality

The same story plays out at the soft edge: $N^{2/3}(\lambda_{\max}-2\sqrt N)$ converges to $F_\beta$ regardless of entry distribution (subject to a sub-Gaussian tail). The Tracy–Widom law is universal.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg=$('#un-svg'), out=$('#un-out');
  const bs={g:$('#un-g'),r:$('#un-r'),u:$('#un-u')};
  const W=720, H=280, ML=50, MR=24, MT=20, MB=44;
  let mode='g';
  function gauss(){
    const u=Math.max(Math.random(),1e-12), v=Math.random();
    return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v);
  }
  function entry(){
    if(mode==='g') return gauss();
    if(mode==='r') return Math.random()<0.5?-1:1;
    if(mode==='u') return (2*Math.random()-1)*Math.sqrt(3);
    return 0;
  }
  // We reuse the tridiagonal trick — but the off-diagonal sub-diagonals are
  // χ_k values, which require Gaussian entries. So we tridiagonalise a
  // dense matrix via Householder — slow for big N, but for N=200 it's fine.
  function buildMatrix(N){
    const A=Array.from({length:N},()=>Array(N).fill(0));
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
      A[i][i]=Math.sqrt(2)*entry();
      for(let j=i+1;j<N;j++){
        const v=entry();
        A[i][j]=v; A[j][i]=v;
      }
    }
    return A;
  }
  function houseTridiag(A){
    const n=A.length;
    const d=Array(n), e=Array(n-1);
    for(let k=0;k<n-2;k++){
      let alpha=0;
      for(let i=k+1;i<n;i++) alpha+=A[i][k]*A[i][k];
      alpha=Math.sqrt(alpha)*(A[k+1][k]>=0?-1:1);
      const r=Math.sqrt(0.5*(alpha*alpha - A[k+1][k]*alpha));
      if(r===0){
        // Degenerate: column k below diagonal is already zero (alpha=0). The
        // column is then already in tridiagonal shape, so set e[k] from the
        // actual sub-diagonal entry and skip the reflection. Measure-zero on
        // Gaussian/Rademacher/uniform entries; the warn surfaces any other
        // case so we know to revisit.
        e[k] = A[k+1][k];
        if (alpha !== 0) console.warn('[rmt-w6] houseTridiag: r=0 with alpha=', alpha, 'at column', k);
        continue;
      }
      const v=Array(n).fill(0);
      v[k+1]=(A[k+1][k]-alpha)/(2*r);
      for(let i=k+2;i<n;i++) v[i]=A[i][k]/(2*r);
      // H = I - 2 v vᵀ
      // A := H A H
      const p=Array(n).fill(0);
      for(let i=k+1;i<n;i++){
        let s=0;
        for(let j=k+1;j<n;j++) s += A[i][j]*v[j];
        p[i]=s;
      }
      let beta=0;
      for(let i=k+1;i<n;i++) beta += v[i]*p[i];
      const q=Array(n).fill(0);
      for(let i=k+1;i<n;i++) q[i]=p[i]-2*beta*v[i];
      for(let i=k+1;i<n;i++){
        for(let j=k+1;j<n;j++){
          A[i][j] -= 2*(v[i]*q[j]+q[i]*v[j]);
        }
      }
      e[k]=alpha;
    }
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++) d[i]=A[i][i];
    if(n>=2) e[n-2]=A[n-1][n-2];
    return {d,e};
  }
  function tridiagEigs(d0,e0){
    const d=d0.slice(), e=e0.slice();
    const n=d.length, eps=1e-12, MAXIT=60*n;
    e.push(0);
    let iter=0;
    for(let l=0;l<n;l++){
      while(iter++<MAXIT){
        let m;
        for(m=l;m<n-1;m++){
          const dd=Math.abs(d[m])+Math.abs(d[m+1]);
          if(Math.abs(e[m])+dd===dd) break;
        }
        if(m===l) break;
        let g=(d[l+1]-d[l])/(2*e[l]);
        const r=Math.hypot(g,1);
        g=d[m]-d[l]+e[l]/(g+(g>=0?r:-r));
        let s=1, c=1, p=0;
        for(let i=m-1;i>=l;i--){
          let f=s*e[i], b=c*e[i];
          const r2=Math.hypot(f,g);
          e[i+1]=r2;
          if(r2===0){ d[i+1]-=p; e[m]=0; break; }
          s=f/r2; c=g/r2;
          g=d[i+1]-p;
          const r3=(d[i]-g)*s + 2*c*b;
          p=s*r3; d[i+1]=g+p; g=c*r3-b;
        }
        if(e[m]!==0 || e[l]!==e[l]){
          d[l]-=p; e[l]=g; e[m]=0;
        }
      }
    }
    return d.sort((a,b)=>a-b);
  }
  function sample(N){
    const A=buildMatrix(N);
    const {d,e}=houseTridiag(A);
    return tridiagEigs(d,e).map(x=>x/Math.sqrt(2*N));
  }
  let eigs=null;
  function render(){
    if(eigs===null) eigs=sample(200);
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const XMIN=-2.5, XMAX=2.5, YMAX=0.45;
    const xpx=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*(v-XMIN)/(XMAX-XMIN);
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/YMAX;
    // grid
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const yv=YMAX*i/4, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // histogram
    const BINS=46;
    const counts=Array(BINS).fill(0);
    for(const x of eigs){
      const b=Math.floor((x-XMIN)/(XMAX-XMIN)*BINS);
      if(b>=0 && b<BINS) counts[b]++;
    }
    const norm=eigs.length*((XMAX-XMIN)/BINS);
    const colour = mode==='g'?'var(--cyan)':mode==='r'?'var(--pink)':'var(--green)';
    for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++){
      const x=xpx(XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*i/BINS), x2=xpx(XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*(i+1)/BINS);
      const y=ypx(counts[i]/norm);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:x+0.5,y,width:x2-x-1,height:Math.max(0,H-MB-y),fill:colour,opacity:0.62}));
    }
    // semicircle
    const p=[];
    for(let k=0;k<=200;k++){
      const x=XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*k/200;
      const r = Math.abs(x)>=2 ? 0 : Math.sqrt(4-x*x)/(2*Math.PI);
      p.push((k?'L':'M')+xpx(x).toFixed(2)+' '+ypx(r).toFixed(2));
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:p.join(' '),fill:'none',stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    // axis
    for(let k=-2;k<=2;k++){
      const x=xpx(k);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:H-MB,x2:x,y2:H-MB+5,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=String(k); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // readout
    const desc={g:'Gaussian N(0,1) entries (above diagonal)',
                r:'Rademacher entries (±1 with prob ½ each), var=1',
                u:'Uniform on [−√3, √3], var=1'};
    let m4=0, m2=0;
    for(const x of eigs){ m2+=x*x; m4+=x*x*x*x; }
    m2/=eigs.length; m4/=eigs.length;
    out.textContent =
      desc[mode]+'\n'+
      'N=200 eigenvalues; rescaled empirical second moment ≈ '+m2.toFixed(3)+' (Wigner: 1)\n'+
      'fourth moment ≈ '+m4.toFixed(3)+' (Wigner C₂=2: ' +
      (Math.abs(m4-2)<0.25?'matches':'still converging') + ')';
  }
  function setMode(m){
    mode=m; eigs=null;
    for(const k of Object.keys(bs)) bs[k].classList.toggle('active', k===m);
    render();
  }
  bs.g.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('g'));
  bs.r.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('r'));
  bs.u.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('u'));
  $('#un-resample').addEventListener('click',()=>{eigs=null; render();});
  setMode('g');
})();
</script>

</section>

7. Katz–Sarnak: random matrices meet $L$-functions

The most arresting universality phenomenon in random matrix theory is not internal — it's a bridge to analytic number theory. The zeros of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line look exactly like eigenvalues of a random unitary matrix.

Montgomery's pair correlation

In 1972 Hugh Montgomery, computing the pair correlation function of the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ under GRH, found a function:

$R_2(\alpha)\;=\;1-\left(\dfrac{\sin\pi\alpha}{\pi\alpha}\right)^2.$

Freeman Dyson, hearing the formula at tea in Princeton, recognised it instantly: it is the pair correlation of GUE eigenvalues. Andrew Odlyzko's massive numerical computations (1987 onward, eventually computing the $10^{20}$-th zero with high precision) confirmed the match to many decimal places.

Katz–Sarnak symmetry types

Nick Katz and Peter Sarnak (1999) elevated this from coincidence to conjecture: every natural family $\mathcal{F}$ of $L$-functions carries a symmetry type from the list

$\{\,U(N),\;O(N)^+,\;O(N)^-,\;\mathrm{USp}(2N)\,\},$

and the low-lying zeros of the family equidistribute against the eigenvalues of a Haar-random matrix in the corresponding compact group. The symmetry type is determined by symmetries of the family:

familysymmetry typelow-zero density
$\zeta(s)$ alone$U$$1-(\sin\pi x/\pi x)^2$
Dirichlet $L(s,\chi_d)$, $\chi_d$ quadratic$\mathrm{USp}$$1-\sin(2\pi x)/(2\pi x)$
$L(s,E)$, $E/\mathbb{Q}$ with $w(E)=+1$$O^+$even orthogonal density
$L(s,E)$, $E/\mathbb{Q}$ with $w(E)=-1$$O^-$odd orthogonal density
$L(s,\mathrm{Sym}^2 f)$, $f$ a cusp form$\mathrm{USp}$same as quadratic-twist family

The symmetry type can usually be predicted from the family's monodromy group on the function-field side: replace $\mathbb{Q}$ by $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$, the $L$-functions become polynomials in $q^{-s}$, and the Frobenius conjugacy class in the geometric monodromy group dictates the matrix-ensemble analogue. Over $\mathbb{Q}$ this is a heuristic; over function fields it's a Deligne–Katz theorem.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg=$('#ks-svg'), out=$('#ks-out');
  const bs={u:$('#ks-u'),sp:$('#ks-sp'),op:$('#ks-op'),om:$('#ks-om')};
  const W=720, H=300, ML=50, MR=24, MT=20, MB=44;
  let mode='u';
  const ZEROS=[14.1347, 21.0220, 25.0109, 30.4249, 32.9351, 37.5862, 40.9187, 43.3271, 48.0052, 49.7738];
  // One-level densities W_G(x) for the four symmetry types (continuous functions of x>=0)
  function density(x,mode){
    const s=Math.PI*x, ss=Math.sin(s);
    if(mode==='u') return 1 - (ss/s)*(ss/s);
    if(mode==='sp'){ // symplectic — density 1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx); no atom (the δ_0 belongs only to O-)
      const t=2*s, st=Math.sin(t);
      return 1 - st/t;
    }
    if(mode==='op'){ // O+ : 1 + sin(2πx)/(2πx)
      const t=2*s, st=Math.sin(t);
      return 1 + st/t;
    }
    if(mode==='om'){ // O- : 1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx) + δ(x)  — we plot the continuous part; visually a deep notch
      const t=2*s, st=Math.sin(t);
      return 1 - st/t;
    }
    return 1;
  }
  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const XMIN=0, XMAX=3, YMAX=1.7;
    const xpx=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*(v-XMIN)/(XMAX-XMIN);
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/YMAX;
    // y-grid
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const yv=YMAX*i/4, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // baseline at 1
    const yOne=ypx(1);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:yOne,x2:W-MR,y2:yOne,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.7,'stroke-dasharray':'3 4'}));
    const t=SVG('text',{x:W-MR-4,y:yOne-4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'}); t.textContent='asymptote = 1'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // density curve (yellow)
    const p=[];
    let started=false;
    for(let k=1;k<=300;k++){
      const x=XMIN+(XMAX-XMIN)*k/300;
      const y=ypx(density(x,mode));
      p.push((started?'L':'M')+xpx(x).toFixed(2)+' '+y.toFixed(2));
      started=true;
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:p.join(' '),fill:'none',stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    // δ-atom indicator for O-
    if(mode==='om'){
      const x0=xpx(0);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x0+1,y1:H-MB,x2:x0+1,y2:MT,stroke:'var(--pink)','stroke-width':2}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:x0+8,y:MT+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--pink)'});
      t.textContent='δ_0  (forced zero at s=½)'; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // zeta zeros as cyan ticks, rescaled so first zero ≈ x=0.5 (illustrative only)
    const scaleZ=14.1347/0.5;
    for(const z of ZEROS){
      const xZ=z/scaleZ;
      if(xZ>=XMIN && xZ<=XMAX){
        const x=xpx(xZ);
        svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:H-MB-12,x2:x,y2:H-MB+2,stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':1.5}));
      }
    }
    // axis
    for(let k=0;k<=3;k++){
      const x=xpx(k);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:H-MB,x2:x,y2:H-MB+5,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=String(k); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    const xlbl=SVG('text',{x:(ML+W-MR)/2,y:H-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    xlbl.textContent='x — zero ordinate / mean zero spacing'; svg.appendChild(xlbl);
    // legend
    const lx=ML+W*0.58, ly=MT+8;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx-6,y:ly-4,width:230,height:48,fill:'var(--panel2)',stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':1,rx:4,opacity:0.92}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+8,x2:lx+18,y2:ly+8,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    let tt=SVG('text',{x:lx+24,y:ly+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); tt.textContent='W_G(x) — one-level density'; svg.appendChild(tt);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+28,x2:lx+18,y2:ly+28,stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':2}));
    tt=SVG('text',{x:lx+24,y:ly+32,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); tt.textContent='first ten ζ-zeros'; svg.appendChild(tt);
    // readout
    const desc={
      u:  'family: {ζ}  →  symmetry type U  →  W(x) = 1 - (sin πx/πx)²  (Montgomery–Odlyzko)',
      sp: 'family: quadratic Dirichlet L(s,χ_d)  →  USp(2N)  →  W(x) = 1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx)  (no atom)',
      op: 'family: E/Q with w(E)=+1  →  O⁺(2N)  →  W(x) = 1 + sin(2πx)/(2πx)  (no forced zero)',
      om: 'family: E/Q with w(E)=-1  →  O⁻(2N+1)  →  W(x) = 1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx) + δ₀  (forced s=½ zero)'
    };
    out.textContent = desc[mode] +
      '\nasymptote W(x) → 1: low-lying zeros average density is the same; the *shape* near 0 distinguishes the symmetry type.';
  }
  function setMode(m){
    mode=m;
    for(const k of Object.keys(bs)) bs[k].classList.toggle('active', k===m);
    render();
  }
  bs.u.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('u'));
  bs.sp.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('sp'));
  bs.op.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('op'));
  bs.om.addEventListener('click',()=>setMode('om'));
  setMode('u');
})();
</script>

blocks.html: What's known, what's conjectured. Over function fields the Katz–Sarnak symmetry assignment is a theorem (Katz–Sarnak; Deligne's equidistribution). Over $\mathbb{Q}$ it's a conjecture, but partial results are striking: the one-level density of the family of quadratic Dirichlet $L$-functions is symplectic for test functions supported in $[-1,1]$ (Özlük–Snyder, Rubinstein); for elliptic-curve $L$-functions the orthogonal-split-by-root-number prediction is supported by Iwaniec–Luo–Sarnak. Soundararajan's $\ge 87.5\%$ non-vanishing of $L(\tfrac12,\chi_d)$ is one of the headline arithmetic consequences. The dictionary in plain English: random matrices are not a metaphor for $L$-functions, they are the conjectured ensemble from which the Frobenius elements are drawn.

See also
  • L-functions and symmetry types
</section>

Connections

Random matrix theory is a hub: born in nuclear physics (Wigner), it has become the universal limit theory for spectral statistics across operator algebras, integrable probability, statistical mechanics, and analytic number theory. The frontier is the marriage of integrability (exactly solvable models like TASEP, last-passage percolation, the KPZ equation) with universality (Tracy–Widom appearing without a closed-form invariant). Free probability is fully alive too — Voiculescu's $\mathrm{Free}(F_n)$ free entropy, the question of whether free group factors $L(F_n)$ are isomorphic for different $n$, the program connecting free probability to large-deviation rate functions — and the Katz–Sarnak picture is still a conjecture over number fields, with concrete special cases proved one family at a time.

  • Probability theory — central limit theorem — the classical CLT is the bulk-of-the-line analogue of the semicircle for sums.
  • High-dimensional geometry — concentration applications — Marchenko–Pastur is the geometric backbone of compressed sensing and high-dimensional statistics.
  • Operator algebras — von Neumann algebras — free probability lives natively in tracial $\mathrm{II}_1$ factors; Voiculescu's free entropy is a $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor invariant.
  • Sato–Tate — the semicircle measure — Sato–Tate's semicircle density for Frobenius angles is the same semicircle, arising from $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-Haar measure on the unit interval.
  • Arithmetic statistics — symmetry types of $L$-function families — the Katz–Sarnak dictionary's number-theory side; Bhargava-style density theorems plug into the same machinery.
  • Spectral graph theory — Ramanujan graphs — Alon–Boppana shows random regular graphs have spectral measure close to Kesten–McKay, the graph analogue of the semicircle.
  • Large deviations — the rate function for eigenvalue fluctuations away from the semicircle is the logarithmic energy: random matrices are a 2D Coulomb gas.
